headline: Law Firms Have Malpractice Insurance. Should Their A.I. Agents?

paragraphs.text: It’s standard practice for lawyers to have malpractice insurance. Ryan Daniels, the founder of the artificial intelligence law firm Crosby, wanted his A.I. agents to have it, too.

The firm relies on A.I. to do the bulk of its contract review work, with about 60 lawyers overseeing the process. It advertises quick turnaround — as little as an hour to review a nondisclosure agreement — at a flat rate.
Crosby’s professional liability policy covers the work of its lawyers and the A.I. tools they supervise. But Daniels wants A.I. agents to handle some tasks without a human in the loop.
“Our goal, ideally by the end of next year, is full legal work done without lawyers — just agents,” he said.

Most insurance companies are not ready to cover A.I. workers. There’s no standard way to assess the risk posed by A.I. tools, and few major carriers offer separate A.I. insurance policies. But many expect A.I. risk to follow the same path as cybersecurity risk, which many carriers excluded from their policies before eventually developing dedicated products.

It took Daniels about six months to secure $5 million of A.I. liability insurance. He eventually landed on Testudo, a two-year-old insurance company with $1 billion of underwriting capacity backed by Lloyd’s of London.

While most law firms aren’t yet buying A.I. coverage (or fully handing off legal work tasks to A.I. agents), the option is increasingly on the radar at all kinds of companies as insurers take steps away from covering A.I. in corporate policies.

“A.I. liability is a growing and emerging exposure that is not contemplated in casualty underwriting really to date,” Evan Greenberg, the C.E.O. of Chubb, said during the insurance company’s most recent earnings call.

The Insurance Services Office, which develops standard policy language, has introduced exclusions for some types of losses caused by generative A.I. They became available for carriers to add to their commercial general liability policies in January.

As of April, at least 16 of the 20 largest liability insurers had filed with state regulators for permission to exclude generative A.I. from policies, according to thousands of filings compiled and analyzed by the investment firm Wolfe Research. Approval gives insurers the option to exclude generative A.I. but doesn’t guarantee they will.

Start-up insurers like Testudo, Harbor and the Artificial Intelligence Underwriting Company have positioned themselves to fill emerging coverage gaps. Many, like Testudo, are backed through Lloyd’s, a specialty insurance marketplace known for insuring new types of risk.

A.I. liability policies may cover losses and legal fees for infringement of intellectual property, bodily injury, property damage, unauthorized data disclosure or output errors caused by generative A.I. Some A.I. insurance start-ups have put more focus on companies that make A.I. tools, and others the end users of those products. Most of Testudo’s clients are longstanding businesses like banks, airports and hospitals, its C.E.O., George Lewin-Smith, said.

Crosby’s policy covers liability for paralegal tasks that can fall into a gray area between clerical work and the practice of law, such as answering a question about a document, reformatting a document, or applying a set of legal playbook rules to a document. If lawyers are approving this type of work, it falls under their professional liability insurance. But there’s little precedent for what happens when an A.I. agent does any sort of legal work without any human involvement.

David Freeman Engstrom, a professor at Stanford Law School who teaches a course on the future of the law firm, said that while a legal malpractice insurance policy could cover the work of unsupervised A.I. agents, “an insurer could argue that a machine output generated without lawyer supervision is not a service rendered ‘as a lawyer’ and so falls outside the policy.”

Eileen Garczynski, a principal at the insurance broker and consultant EPIC Law Firms, conducts an annual survey of senior leaders who manage legal malpractice claims at insurance carriers. While virtually no legal malpractice insurers have excluded lawyers’ supervised use of A.I., she said, they are asking more questions about it.

This year’s survey included 13 providers of legal professional liability insurance, which together cover more than 80 percent of the largest 200 law firms. Seven said they had seen an increase in A.I.-related claims in the last year.
“The legal malpractice insurers were like: ‘OK, we’ve actually had some of these cases now. They’re hallucination cases. What else could be coming?’” she said.

After Crosby’s A.I. liability policy went into effect this week, the company removed all lawyer supervision from its gray-area tasks, which it says account for about 20 percent of its work. It still has lawyers supervising tasks that are clearly legal work.

While Crosby’s goal is for its A.I. agents to practice law autonomously, taking lawyers completely out of the loop would violate regulations. State law prohibits, and in most states criminalizes, practicing law without a license, and state ethics rules require lawyers to supervise nonlawyers, including paralegals and outside vendors, who assist in delivering legal services. In September, California passed a law that stipulates “an attorney shall not delegate the practice of law to generative artificial intelligence.”
Still, there is a gray area between which tasks do and do not need to be supervised by a lawyer, Engstrom said.

Daniels is betting that the rules will evolve. “We assume that at some point in the next year or two, our associations are going to start to relax what agents can do, because they can clearly do legal work,” he said. “And we want to be ahead of the curve and say, ‘Hey, look, our agents can do this, and they’re already insured.’”

Start-ups have developed new approaches to underwriting insurance for artificial intelligence. Some, like AIUC, which also offers a safety and security certification, perform audits of the company’s guardrails and policies, and runs tests that involve thousands of replicas of real-world incidents where A.I. has failed. Testudo’s approach relies more heavily on profiling a company’s liability risks. (For example, a law firm in one location may have a greater risk of being sued than a law firm of similar size based somewhere else.) But it also involves analysis of A.I. technology, guardrails and procedures.

At some types of A.I. companies, one difficulty is the sheer scale of potential damages that could cross different types of insurance policies. Anthropic noted in its S-1 that the scale of harm that could be caused by its technology potentially exceeds the entire insurance industry’s capacity to underwrite, and that “the insurance market for A.I.-specific risks is nascent and evolving, and we may be unable to obtain coverage for certain A.I.-related liabilities on commercially reasonable terms, or at all.”

Another complexity is that assigning liability isn’t always clear-cut: Should the end user, the vendor of an A.I. tool, the maker of the underlying A.I. model or some combination be responsible for damages?
At the same time, the technology is fairly new, and changing quickly.

Neil Kessler, the C.E.O. of the specialty and benefits division at CRC Group, one of the largest wholesale insurance brokers, said there was no way to validate which approach to underwriting A.I. risk was best until more lawsuits played out.
“You won t be able figure out which of the factors drove the losses until you’ve had the losses,” he said.
IN CASE YOU MISSED IT

The jobs report came in stronger than expected. Employers added 165,000 jobs in October, and the unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1 percent. Job gains for August and September were revised upward. The strong report underscored the job market’s stability even as inflation pressures other parts of the economy, and could add to calls for the Federal Reserve to raise its benchmark lending rate next month.

Stocks rallied after a major A.I. sell-off. After Democratic midterm victories agitated investor fears of tighter A.I. regulation, the S&P 500 slumped to its worst daily decline on Thursday since April 2025. Stocks reversed some of those losses on Friday, capping a week of volatility.

A big question emerges over how Democrats will use their power. The party won majorities in both the House and Senate, as well as key governorships across the country. Speculation swirled over what that will mean for government oversight of A.I. and data centers, cryptocurrency, health care, prediction markets and more. And with a stunning sweep by Texas Democrats, what will happen to the state’s efforts to loosen regulations on corporations?
More big deals: Tesla is winding down production of its Cybertruck. CVS plans to split off its drugstore business. And Stephen Miller replaced Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff.
The power of the price tag

Americans made clear this Election Day that they’re fed up with the rising cost of living, and Lindsay Owens thinks she has one solution: cracking down on dynamic pricing, the now common practice of adjusting prices in real time.

That call — including in her new book, “Gouged” — by Owens, the president and C.E.O. of the left-of-center Washington think tank Groundwork Collaborative, is catching attention both in corporate boardrooms and on Capitol Hill. Walmart has fired back, accusing her of misrepresenting how it does business.
Owens spoke with Nancy Scola about the power of the price tag and why she’s so concerned about what she sees as algorithms’ growing role in how we shop.
Should I care about dynamic pricing because it’s going to cost me more or because it feels unfair?
Pricing has gone high-tech, and it has changed the consumer experience.

Prices are higher but also more volatile. You used to be able to pull out a Sunday circular and know how much milk was going to cost for the week. Now you may not be able to trust the price of milk is going to stay the same for the entire trip to the grocery store.
Is the concern I get charged more for an umbrella because it’s raining, I live in a nice neighborhood or a retailer suspects I’m more worried about getting my hair wet than my bald neighbor?
I’m a big fan of charging a fair price for the umbrella. A fair price is how much it costs to make, plus a margin competed down in a competitive market.
Charging people who have hair spray on their hair more is not the economy I want to live in. I don’t think it’s the economy most Americans want to live in.

You’ve been going back and forth with Walmart. C.E.O. John Furner has insisted that “we price the product, not the person.” The company also argues that data-driven pricing goes back to the days of Sam Walton.

The story of the price tag in America begins in Philadelphia. John Wanamaker was said to be inspired by the Quakers, who felt it wasn’t equitable to haggle. The price tag has been a critical piece of the infrastructure of comparison shopping since the 1870s.
It beggars belief to suggest Sam Walton would endorse the pricing technologies Walmart has built and patented.
Say you wake up tomorrow the C.E.O. of Walmart. Is your policy to charge customers the exact same price no matter where they are?
You pay more in Hawaii because it costs more to get stuff to Hawaii. But broadly speaking, the price online, in the app, in the store should be the same.
Retailers say electronic shelf labels just make it more efficient to update prices. They shouldn’t have the benefit of that innovation?
I have no problem with any of the technologies themselves. I have a problem with how companies use the technologies.

They’re running experiments to see under what conditions they can get us to pay the absolute maximum. And if you don’t believe them or me, you should believe the companies they buy to facilitate these experiments. They advertise the revenue maximization potential — not the discounting potential.
One example you give is how the Savannah Bananas barnstorming baseball team tries to keep ticket prices steady and low, about $60. What lessons do you draw?
They sell out stadiums major league franchises have a tough time selling out. They have a cult following. It’s not a charity situation. They’re doing quite well.
Is pricing the real driver of Americans’ economic angst or a useful way of focusing their attention?

The ways in which companies’ pricing power manifests in our economy is particularly poignant and resonant. Everything Americans grew up understanding about pricing has changed. Big Tech reinvented the rip-off.

It is time to re-evaluate how comfortable we are with these new approaches. Consumer backlash is actually a really important way in which markets are disciplined and companies are told, “Hey, you’ve touched the stove.”
How did prediction markets do?
Polymarket and Kalshi have advertised that their markets are better at predicting the outcome of elections than polls and election forecasts.
According to an analysis by The New York Times, using statistical methods, how did the accuracy of prediction markets compare with traditional methods over the last three months before the midterms?
